title: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
desc: Treats legal AI as multidisciplinary organizational change requiring leadership, frontline resources, connected data and concrete workflow problems.

kps.k: The cluster treats legal AI as organisational and service redesign, not a software purchase.
kps.d: The central proposition is that model capability creates possibilities, while leadership, incentives, workflows, infrastructure and learning determine whether organisations realise value. Niles, Ciesla, Microsoft’s Rebecca Anderson and the Cooley CEO argue that isolated pilots and individual efficiency gains leave the delivery model largely untouched. Um connects AI investment to competitive strategy. Moving beyond pilots therefore means integrating experimentation into core services, not abandoning testing. These accounts advance a strategic prescription rather than establish one successful replacement model.

qs.q: Buying tools is honestly not the answer, it’s just part of the answer and it should be delivered as a joined up change strategy.
qs.a: Revenue Leakage, Metadata, and the Post Billable Hour Playbook, Stefan Ciesla of Ayora · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: But the thing that I would encourage leaders of law firms to think about is, AI is not just a tool, it's an operating model.
qs.a: Inside Microsoft Legal: A Look at AI Use Built for Scale (Rebecca Anderson - Head of Legal EMEA Microsoft) · In-house counsel · 2026

kps.k: Economic incentives, workload and professional identity explain resistance better than a single claim of technological conservatism.
kps.d: Um argues that financially pressured segments adopted new delivery methods earlier, while incumbent profitability weakens urgency. Leonard identifies two hourly-billing disincentives: experimentation displaces revenue, and successful efficiency can reduce billable work. Crosby’s Daniels instead ranks partner distributions and short investment horizons above hourly billing. In-house departments face different pressures to control costs and accelerate business activity. Wilkins and Marwaha add anxiety about professional identity and support-role displacement. Lambert rejects age as a sufficient explanation, and Skoghag reports openness when organisations prepare change well. These mechanisms do not imply that individual associates deliberately work slowly.

qs.q: You have to be willing to invest that time by taking a hit to your revenue, and recognize that ultimately you might be taking a bigger hit to your revenue if you find efficiencies through what you're learning in AI.
qs.a: Can Judges Use AI? Inside the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's Interim Policy — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: So it's really hard for them to allocate money that they could take home today um to long-term innovation.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

kps.k: Leadership and frontline experimentation are complementary, but participation requires resources and credible recognition.
kps.d: Accounts differ on whether leaders or individual users initiate adoption. Harvey’s founders describe early lawyer enthusiasm preceding leadership commitment; other practitioners report top-down directives. AAA’s innovation pipeline and Thomson Reuters’ champions programme connect staff ideas to central priorities. Quinn Emanuel reports voluntary cross-functional learning without initial billable-time credit, whereas Leonard reports Ropes & Gray allowing up to 400 hours of AI experimentation toward associate targets. Um argues that demanding billing requirements make unsupported exploration unreasonable. The practical issue is sustaining participation beyond enthusiastic early users through protected time, implementation support, transparent plans and permission to report failure.

qs.q: And then on the flip side these incredible ideas that they're coming up with are being fed back to the central AI strategy team.
qs.a: Norie Campbell & Jen Ruddick — Thomson Reuters legal department (GCO 2030) · In-house counsel · 2026

qs.q: There was no credit or billable time given; it was just, “If you want to learn about this, mess around with it, and share your findings, join in.” There was tons of enthusiasm, and it was really, really rewarding.
qs.a: Building an AI-Forward Law Firm: Lessons from Quinn Emanuel — full episode transcript · Law firms · 2025

kps.k: The debate disputes the scale and sequence of change, while converging on concrete client and workflow problems.
kps.d: Leonard and McCormack advocate ambitious workstream redesign; other speakers favour small, measurable improvements and sequential bottleneck removal. McCormack offers a bridge: initial efficiency can create time for further exploration. Shaver recommends concentrated investment in distinctive expertise or important clients, and Ruddick reports stronger progress after narrowing priorities. Sunderman recommends checking existing technology and organisational readiness before buying more. Reeves and the litigation-workflow discussion emphasise observing actual practice, information flows and handoffs. These accounts support deliberate discovery rather than indiscriminate deployment, but do not quantify which implementation sequence works best.

qs.q: So now, it’s sort of “take big swings, and learn what you can learn, and then scale back.”
qs.a: Training the Next Generation of Lawyers: How AI Is Redefining Legal Training — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: We have to think in terms of baby steps and progress that is measurable and verifiable and we can bring everyone along with us.
qs.a: Talking AI for Access to Justice at the 25th Innovations in Technology Conference — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

kps.k: Useful systems require multidisciplinary implementation, connected data and explicit legal expertise.
kps.d: Crosby describes lawyers and engineers refining real workflows and individual outputs together. Cleary, Legora and Harvey report technical integration and practitioner-led implementation support. Fleisher stresses use-case-specific access to business context; Barnwell hypothesises that articulating tacit professional heuristics can make them usable by AI. Pike argues that rapid prototyping lets some lawyers test ideas before obtaining specialist resources, not that every lawyer becomes a developer. Shared platforms therefore need not eliminate differentiation: firms may compete through expertise, client context and reusable services. Productising that expertise remains conditional on reliability, data permissions, confidentiality, privilege and viable economics.

qs.q: You really have to think about each use case and what type of data you need and where that data lives.
qs.a: How AI Is Reshaping In-House Legal Teams with Nick Fleisher — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: AI, you were kind of in the same position where everyone bought the same legal tech, but the differentiation really came from your lawyers, how you run your law firm, how you structure your practices.
qs.a: The Models Are the Product: Gabe Pereyra on Building an AI Associate and Matter-Centric Workflows · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Buyer-side adoption can redistribute work and make joint delivery design more important.
kps.d: Moderna’s Klinger reports preparing more sophisticated licensing drafts internally and commissioning focused outside review, with unquantified savings. Microsoft expects outside counsel to explain how their AI strategy applies to its work. Axiom and Harvey describe coordination among in-house teams, firms and ALSPs, rather than universal insourcing. Nadler counters that busy departments may lack time to build automation. Proposed value extends beyond fewer hours to speed, predictability, stronger work and legal requirements embedded in business operations. These examples establish reported changes in work allocation, not market-wide displacement or demonstrated improvements in client outcomes.

qs.q: We do many more first drafts now even of sophisticated licensing agreements and then send them to our outside deal council and say can you please spend an hour on this and can you look at the following provisions that has been fantastic from an efficiency and cost savings perspective.
qs.a: Shannon Thyme Klinger — Moderna (Chief Legal Officer) on rewiring a legal function around AI · In-house counsel · 2025

qs.q: And more than that, we want to have open and transparent conversations about what is their AI strategy, how does their AI strategy play out in our work.
qs.a: Inside Microsoft Legal: A Look at AI Use Built for Scale (Rebecca Anderson - Head of Legal EMEA Microsoft) · In-house counsel · 2026

kps.k: Commercial accountability remains in tension with the need to learn before returns are clear.
kps.d: Leonard interprets some unsuccessful pilots as part of an early learning phase and questions premature firm-wide ROI demands. Wakeling recommends terminating projects unlikely to earn money; Junestrand favours task-level measurement while acknowledging aggregation difficulties. AAA prioritises service quality and reach rather than profit alone. Pricing proposals include fixed fees, reusable services and mixed delivery models, but no settled successor to hourly billing emerges. Assessment should distinguish licences, sustained use, task quality, turnaround, human intervention, total implementation costs, client value and financial return. Higher usage or shorter task time alone cannot establish organisational success.

qs.q: And the media takeaway of that report was like, “This is all hype and not really something worth investing in,” whereas what I took from it is the contrary: everybody's playing with it in their own space, and it's not yet ready in most cases for highly structured, measured ROI, because everybody just has to learn to build a muscle around it.
qs.a: AI in LA Courts: David Slayton on Access to Justice — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: And so our mission is to make sure we kill the things which are never gonna make money.
qs.a: Talking about the Future of AI in Law with David Wakeling · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Governance must evolve with deployment while preserving substantive verification and task-specific controls.
kps.d: Kercher reports fabricated quotations and facts in internal drafts and requires substantive checking before reliance. Fleisher recommends approval steps for consequential external actions; Microsoft describes human-defined decision points, and Norm Law reports attorney supervision before client delivery. These approaches distinguish lawyer augmentation from direct reliance on autonomous output. Leonard warns against rigid frameworks, while McCormack raises audits, model changes and dependence on underlying providers. Practical proposals include escalation routes, incident learning, client tabletop exercises and interdisciplinary oversight. McCormack’s suggestion that useful AI might eventually become necessary for competence is conditional, not a universal current duty to use it.

qs.q: I’ve been burned a few times in internal drafts where I thought I had a great quote or fact, and it turned out the model just fabricated it.
qs.a: Building an AI-Forward Law Firm: Lessons from Quinn Emanuel — full episode transcript · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: I think in those, you want to see more human-in-the-loop steps, where you have to press approve on anything that the agent is going to go do.
qs.a: How AI Is Reshaping In-House Legal Teams with Nick Fleisher — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Training and career design must change, but the replacement pathway to professional judgment remains unresolved.
kps.d: Klinger warns that insourcing removes developmental assignments from firms. Crane and McCormack question whether increasingly leveraged apprenticeship reliably supplied mentoring, while Dhein disputes the educational value of some repetitive tasks. Proposed alternatives include simulations, feedback, competency frameworks, client exposure and participation in tool development. Boyko retains human mentorship; Schwarcz recommends legal foundations before structured AI training. Predictions about junior readiness conflict, and Hoffman warns against shifting employers’ training responsibilities to schools. Hybrid roles also require recognition, advancement and inclusive participation. Reports of frustrated innovation leaders and scarce transition talent support attention to role design, not guarantees that AI expertise protects employment.

qs.q: But that means basically we are doing the mid to senior level associate work enabled by technology that was the very work that trained young lawyers that that I trained on as a litigator that our deal lawyers trained on as young lawyers.
qs.a: Shannon Thyme Klinger — Moderna (Chief Legal Officer) on rewiring a legal function around AI · In-house counsel · 2025

qs.q: You could say, “I want to run a simulated fund formation, a simulated litigation, a simulated merger,” and go through the process end to end, getting feedback from a simulated client and simulated partners.
qs.a: Harvey's Gabe Pereyra on the Future of Legal AI · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: AI-enabled capacity does not determine firm size, employment or competitive winners.
kps.d: AI-native providers describe structures built around technical collaboration and new delivery economics. Abramowitz leaves open whether these entrants or better-executing incumbents pose the greater threat. Pereyra expects improved coordination to support larger firms and stresses full-service incumbents’ breadth; other speakers envisage expert boutiques, fewer execution roles or reduced lawyer demand. Unmet demand and new work might absorb capacity, but aggregate employment effects remain unestablished. Smaller providers may gain capabilities while facing training, capital and specialist-staff constraints; costly customisation could favour consolidation. Client savings, wider service and improved wellbeing depend on deliberate allocation of gains.

qs.q: Whether that threat ends up being AI-first firms or traditional firms that execute better — that remains to be seen.
qs.a: AI Agents and the Widening Divide in Legal with Zach Abramowitz — full episode transcript · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: I expect what you’ll see is that there will actually be much larger law firms, because I think this technology will let you scale law firms much more the same way Salesforce did with sales organizations.
qs.a: When Will Lawyers Trust AI? — Gabe Pereyra (Harvey) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Public-service redesign must address unmet legal need without treating human assistance as dispensable.
kps.d: Slayton argues that courts should compare AI risks with failures in the existing system, not an ideal risk-free alternative. Court Help provides a concrete informational-triage example, with escalation to people when needed. Legal-aid discussions report active experimentation, but anticipated capacity gains remain expectations rather than measured results. Brown and Moon prioritise human interaction, while McCormack calls for user participation and transparency. Garfield’s reported narrow direct-service authorisation differs from lawyer augmentation and does not establish unrestricted permission elsewhere. Funding tied to hours, limited public resources and institutional capacity to handle additional claims complicate implementation.

qs.q: A system without AI—a system without new technology—has failures and risks as well, and they are significant.
qs.a: AI in LA Courts: David Slayton on Access to Justice — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: And so one of the questions centered on how likely do you think, well, looking ahead, if you were using AI to its full potential to speed time consuming tasks, how many more clients, percentage wise do you estimate your organization could serve?
qs.a: Why Is Legal Aid Embracing AI Faster than Other Legal Professionals? — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

kps.k: The evidence establishes experimentation and uneven implementation more clearly than causal transformation effects.
kps.d: Most support comes from practitioner experience, company-reported programmes, customer conversations and forecasts. Quinn’s reported uptake, associate-built tools, Microsoft’s intake changes and Moderna’s drafting workflow demonstrate activity, but do not isolate productivity, quality or financial effects. Repeated accounts do not provide independent corroboration. Schwarcz’s experimental findings add an important qualification: AI may improve short-term unaided understanding for some participants, yet AI-assisted final revision worsened stronger participants’ work. Those results do not settle long-term learning effects. Task-specific findings, incomplete survey methods and changing models argue for repeated assessment and against uniform adoption timetables or claims of universal superiority.

qs.q: We're a nonprofit with a mission to serve, but it's going to be a while before we can disaggregate all the different things going on and figure out where to credit the technology versus the people empowered by the technology, or both.
qs.a: Can Judges Use AI? Inside the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's Interim Policy — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: But I think the positive story is that AI can actually allow junior associates who, without the aid of AI, might struggle to understand or apply certain materials, not only to produce better work, but then to be better advocates and lawyers when they don’t have the AI.
qs.a: Can AI Make Lawyers Better? — Daniel Schwarcz · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The curated AI-native legal-provider sources accept the proposition that legal AI is principally a service and organisational redesign challenge, and collectively develop it with concrete operating-model proposals. Recurring reasons include the need to organise delivery around defined client pain points rather than generic tools; embed lawyers, engineers and AI specialists in shared workflows; connect operational data and systems; redesign investment, pricing and recognition incentives; and retain lawyer direction, testing and human oversight. Crosby most explicitly links multidisciplinary teams to workflow instrumentation and argues that partnership distributions impede long-term investment. Norm Law stresses that busy in-house teams often lack the capacity to automate even when given tools. Covenant proposes direct-to-client, software-first delivery with embedded legal expertise, while Garfield adds connected accounting data and intensive scenario-based testing. Material variation concerns emphasis and expected pace: some sources advocate substantial AI-first reconstruction and extensive workflow offloading, whereas Mazares anticipates gradual, uneven change and Kemnitz foregrounds durable human creativity and supervision. Sources also differ on whether incumbent incentives, leadership selection, client pressure or implementation capacity is the dominant constraint. Competitive outcomes between AI-native providers, vendors, in-house teams and adapting incumbents remain unresolved. Most evidence consists of provider descriptions, practitioner observations, analogies and forecasts rather than independently measured productivity, quality or financial effects.

qs.q: They're being handed all these AI tools and there's this direction to figure out how to automate, but no one that's not long AI the way we are has the time really in their day to do that.
qs.a: AI First Firms Joining the AmLaw 100 is 'Inevitable' — Batya Nadler (Partner, Norm Law) on Legally Disrupted ep. 55 · AI-native providers · 2026

vlens.an: The curated academia and research sources accept the proposition that legal AI is an organisational and service-design challenge rather than merely a software purchase, and materially develop it in three ways. First, they specify multidisciplinary implementation structures: lawyer–engineer design partnerships, engineers embedded in deal teams, participation by legal information professionals, and cross-disciplinary decision-making. Second, they extend redesign into professional formation, advocating legal foundations before structured AI use, tool-agnostic education, direct observation of practice and continuing reassessment as models change. Third, they connect implementation choices to broader outcomes including bias, public trust, access to justice and institutional resilience. Common reasoning is that useful and responsible adoption depends on complementary expertise, intentional design, practical experimentation and users capable of evaluating outputs. Material variation concerns emphasis and evidentiary strength: Schwarcz contributes task-specific experimental findings showing heterogeneous effects across participants, whereas most other sources offer recommendations, professional observations, exploratory workshops or forecasts rather than measured implementation results. Some focus narrowly on education and professional development; others propose concrete workflow or service models, including agentic legal-aid administration and AI-assisted general-counsel decision-making. Hoffman is more cautious about stable notions of AI-readiness and stresses institutional and regulatory resistance, but remains directionally aligned. Collectively, these sources deepen the proposition without establishing that any particular redesign model is generally effective.

qs.q: Lawyers don't know what engineers are able to do, so what we have to figure out is some very, very tight working collaboration, design partnerships between lawyers and engineers, software developers, IT professionals and computer science researchers in order to build these tools.
qs.a: Law as Code & the AI Power Shift · Academia · 2026

qs.q: But those risks are risks that must be managed and addressed in a thoughtful way, as opposed to simply forgoing the underlying activity that creates the risk—which is the use of AI.
qs.a: Can AI Make Lawyers Better? — Daniel Schwarcz · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: These selected access-to-justice and civil-society sources accept the cluster’s principal proposition that legal AI is an organisational and service-redesign challenge, then materially extend it by specifying public-service design priorities: compare AI-assisted help with unmet need rather than ideal representation; organise assistance around problem recognition, triage, escalation and delivery; preserve or maximise human interaction; support pro bono lawyers with client-specific preparation; and reconsider funding tied to hours. Common reasons include severe resource scarcity, pressure from the justice gap, professional risk aversion and identity, implementation constraints, and the need for leadership, experimentation and staff support. Material variation concerns pace and mode: some advocate urgent experimentation or ambitious end-to-end pathways, while others favour small, measurable steps, lower-risk internal uses and longer implementation timelines. Some contemplate direct-to-consumer assistance where no lawyer is available, whereas others emphasise copilot use and technology that facilitates rather than replaces people. The sources mostly offer project descriptions, expectations and practical judgments—not measured access-to-justice outcomes—so they strengthen the cluster’s service-design account without establishing causal improvements in reach, quality or wellbeing.

qs.q: But again, as sort of things evolve and the feedback that we hear from people, I really realize that this is a human endeavor that we’re on and we’re just using technology or we should just be using technology as a tool to facilitate those interactions instead of offloading them.
qs.a: What Is Human-Centered Legal Help in the Age of AI? — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: If funding is based on the number of hours people spend doing certain kinds of work, and this technology undercuts that, then it’s not just rethinking the billable hour, but it’s rethinking how we acknowledge and fund value and service that is created for clients, right?
qs.a: Talking AI for Access to Justice at the 25th Innovations in Technology Conference — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

vlens.an: These curated traditional-law-firm sources consistently accept the cluster’s principal proposition that legal AI is an organisational and service-redesign challenge rather than a software purchase. Collectively, they materially develop it with concrete implications for firm strategy, workflow discovery, implementation staffing, multidisciplinary technical capability, governance, pricing and lawyer development. Common reasoning is that model capability produces value only when firms align leadership, people, processes and client needs: Quinn Emanuel centres practising lawyers’ real workflow problems and dedicated implementation support; Cleary adds technologists, client design partnerships and risk calibration; Boyko and Dhein connect adoption to redesigned training while preserving human responsibility for mentorship and judgment; Cooley and Maziarek extend redesign to pricing, value creation and the legal product itself. Material variation concerns sequence and emphasis rather than the core proposition. Quinn describes voluntary bottom-up experimentation, Rachel stresses incremental people-first change, and other sources favour more explicit strategic or leadership-led transformation. Boyko retains systematic human mentorship, whereas Dhein mainly challenges the educational value of repetitive junior tasks without specifying a replacement pathway. Commercial views range from task-level process improvement and predictability to broader movement away from time-based pricing. The evidentiary basis is also limited: these accounts largely offer practitioner experience, anecdotes and forecasts, not controlled evidence that any particular redesign improves productivity, quality, financial returns or employment outcomes. They therefore strengthen the proposition chiefly by supplying implementation models and organisational requirements, not by establishing a generally successful transformation model for traditional firms.

qs.q: It’s not very effective to have people far removed from day-to-day practice dictate, “Here’s exactly how you shall use AI.” Instead, we let the practicing lawyers guide how AI gets implemented in their workflows.
qs.a: Building an AI-Forward Law Firm: Lessons from Quinn Emanuel — full episode transcript · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: Pricing must increasingly reflect value created rather than time spent, whether tied to business or legal outcomes, risk mitigation, speed, or greater predictability.
qs.a: Cooley CEO: Big Law Won't Survive if It Treats AI as Just an Efficiency Tool · Law firms · 2026

vlens.an:
This curated legal-tech-vendor voice accepts the cluster’s principal proposition and, overall, materially develops it. The recurring argument is that model capability or licence purchase is insufficient: value depends on redesigning workflows and services around concrete client problems, integrating legal and technical expertise, providing training and implementation support, connecting relevant data, and aligning leadership, trust, pricing and professional incentives. Several sources supply concrete mechanisms beyond the proposition itself, including shared buyer-provider workspaces, lawyer-led prototyping, legal-engineering teams, productised expertise, attorney-supervised agents, workflow mapping, client co-development and upstream embedding of legal requirements in business operations.

Material variation concerns emphasis and ambition rather than basic direction. Some sources foreground adoption mechanics—guided use, champions, hands-on experimentation and change leadership—while others propose more structural changes, such as scalable legal products, AI-native delivery models, new pricing relationships or in-house lawyers becoming architects of business workflows. Accounts also differ on whether adoption begins with executives or frontline lawyers, and on whether implementation should proceed through incremental bottleneck removal or broader service redesign. A smaller set concentrates mainly on vendor-side iteration, product simplicity or general capability and therefore redirects or leaves the organisational proposition unclear rather than contradicting it. Across the material, predictions of rapid transformation and large productivity gains are less well supported than the descriptions of experimentation and implementation practice: most evidence comes from company experience, customer conversations and anecdotes, not independent measurements of quality, financial return or organisation-wide outcomes.

qs.q: Buying tools is honestly not the answer, it’s just part of the answer and it should be delivered as a joined up change strategy.
qs.a: Revenue Leakage, Metadata, and the Post Billable Hour Playbook, Stefan Ciesla of Ayora · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: They come in with a mindset that’s like, I used to know how it was practicing in this practice area, and now with AI, we can totally reshape the way that work gets done.** And we want to help figure that out.
qs.a: Max Junestrand, Legora: 'We're Setting the Precedent' · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

vlens.an: Within this curated set, the market-analyst, consultancy and press sources accept the proposition that legal AI adoption is primarily organisational and service redesign rather than software procurement, and materially develop it with practical mechanisms. Common explanations for uneven adoption include misaligned commercial incentives, protected partner economics, heavy billable workloads, limited capital, weak leadership trust, inadequate training and governance, and anxiety that efficiency may diminish professional value. Their prescriptions include aligning AI with competitive strategy, defining client and workflow problems, inventorying existing technology, resourcing frontline experimentation, using domain experts, redesigning delivery and pricing, and testing commercial returns. Material variation concerns scale and sequence: some envisage AI-first firms abandoning traditional leverage and possibly hourly billing, while others favour selective customisation, readiness checks and incremental experiments. They also differ on whether competitive threats or internal learning should drive change, and on how quickly to demand returns. Governance-focused sources counsel slower agentic deployment, while more optimistic accounts predict rapid cumulative learning and widening competitive gaps. These claims are mostly experiential, anecdotal or predictive; the sources themselves often acknowledge uncertainty, mixed implementation and the absence of demonstrated transformation effects.

qs.q: What I’m trying to show with these examples is that you can’t have an AI strategy that’s separate from your competitive strategy.
qs.a: The 2026 Am Law 100 Power Rankings — Jae Um · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: In fact, we’ve glorified working 12 hours a day for so many years, you are so nervous about going down to eight hours a day because you don’t think you’re gonna be value add anymore.
qs.a: Kenzo Tsushima of Morae on Innovation, Change Management, and Servant Leadership · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an:
This curated set of regulators, court leaders and professional-body voices generally accepts the proposition that legal AI is an organisational and service-redesign challenge, then materially extends it into public institutions, professional education and regulatory architecture. Common reasons include the need for mission-led leadership, protected staff time, frontline and user participation, multidisciplinary legal-technical teams, connected institutional data, workflow-specific experimentation, training, transparency and risk-tiered human oversight. Court-focused sources particularly add public-funding and staffing constraints, preservation of litigants’ voices, access-to-justice goals and comparison of AI risks with harms already present in the justice system. Professional-body and education sources develop competency frameworks, assessment reform and cross-institutional training, while AAA accounts provide concrete innovation pipelines, hybrid roles and blank-slate case-management redesign.

Material variation concerns both ambition and emphasis. Some favour bounded, low-risk assistance with human review or appeal; others contemplate automated resolution or direct AI services for narrow, high-volume matters. Several focus on practical organisational implementation, whereas McCormack’s regulatory discussion redirects attention toward public AI use, unauthorized-practice boundaries and potentially outdated regulatory architecture. Sources also differ on whether to begin with incremental measurable pilots or ambitious end-to-end redesign. Across these positions, claimed productivity, access and financial benefits remain mostly prospective, anecdotal or organisation-reported rather than demonstrated causal outcomes. This synthesis characterises only the supplied curated sources, not regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: The tech is much easier to learn than the change-management piece, I think.
qs.a: Live from Legal Week 2025: Unveiling a New AI Course for Lawyers — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: And that is thinking about really starting from scratch, examining all of our workflows and trying to really think of it as a blank slate.
qs.a: An AI Arbitrator? The Latest Innovations from the American Arbitration Association, with CEO Bridget McCormack and CTO Diana Didia · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an:
The curated in-house counsel and legal-operations sources consistently accept the proposition that legal AI is an organisational and service-design challenge rather than a standalone software purchase. Their common reasoning is that adoption depends on executive accountability, organisational support, defined business outcomes, workflow selection, change management, training and permission to experiment. They also emphasise connecting frontline use to a central strategy and measuring legal’s contribution to business objectives rather than activity alone.

Material variation concerns emphasis and consequences, not the proposition’s validity. Darr foregrounds whether the wider organisation gives legal leaders the structure and support needed to implement change. Campbell and Ruddick favour a focused roadmap, champions and continuous learning; Logvinova and Vaughn stress leadership-led engagement and workforce upskilling; Niles stresses executive accountability and redesign of client-service delivery; and Anderson frames AI as an operating model built around outcomes, organisational knowledge, governed agents and redesigned intake. Klinger goes further into buyer-provider effects: AI-enabled insourcing can narrow outside counsel’s assignment and disrupt the traditional training pipeline, requiring joint redesign by legal departments and firms. The sources also differ on workforce expectations: Klinger highlights risks to junior development, whereas Campbell is more concerned about established lawyers’ adaptability. These accounts principally provide practitioner experience, prescriptions and predictions; they offer limited quantified evidence of causal productivity, quality or financial outcomes.

qs.q: But the thing that I would encourage leaders of law firms to think about is, AI is not just a tool, it's an operating model.
qs.a: Inside Microsoft Legal: A Look at AI Use Built for Scale (Rebecca Anderson - Head of Legal EMEA Microsoft) · In-house counsel · 2026

qs.q: But if I didn't have all that support it wouldn't happen.
qs.a: Elaine Darr — DHL Supply Chain (VP Legal & Regulatory Affairs) on legal ops, trained models, and market-rate billing enforcement · In-house counsel · 2025

elens.an:
The curated 2023–2024 sources consistently accept the proposition that generative AI adoption is organisational and service redesign rather than a discrete software purchase, and collectively make material extensions to it. Their common reasoning is that useful adoption depends on leadership, protected learning time, workforce participation, AI literacy, multidisciplinary input and selection of concrete client or workflow problems. Several sources also locate resistance in billable-hour incentives, workload, professional risk aversion, expert overconfidence and fear when automation reaches work lawyers regard as core. The period adds concrete implementation models: AAA’s staff-to-innovation pipeline; mission-aligned and adaptive strategy; bottom-up associate participation; client-specific pro bono preparation; selective human-in-the-loop judicial uses; and redesign proposals for courts, legal education and women’s career pathways.

Material variation concerns scope, sequence and institutional setting rather than the core proposition. Some sources advocate reimagining entire workstreams, whereas others recommend bounded experiments, small exploratory teams or task-specific case selection. Courts, small practices and public-service organisations stress funding, training and technical-capacity constraints; law-firm discussions place more weight on billable-hour incentives and professional identity; in-house sources anticipate earlier pressure from their parent businesses. Some contributions focus on augmentation and preserving human judgment, voice and transparency, while others envisage more automated low-stakes dispute resolution. Expectations about productivity, access to justice, employment and business-model change are generally predictive or anecdotal, not measured causal findings. The sources give comparatively limited attention to connected data, formal verification systems and commercial outcome measurement, and they do not establish a successful general replacement model.

qs.q: We move those ideas to Go Teams for design sprints, gather user data and input—customer discovery—and then move things quickly through an innovation pipeline into practice.
qs.a: Transforming Law with AI: Generative Models, Innovation in Dispute Resolution, and Leadership in Change — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: One of the things I talk about a lot is monodisciplinarity—the fact that all of our systems and organizations have to be owned and led by lawyers means that we miss out on insights from other disciplines.
qs.a: Can AI Replace Human Judgment? Medicine, Law, and the Future — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that legal AI at scale is principally an organisational and service-redesign challenge, then materially develop it with implementation detail. Common explanations are that model access alone does not change delivery: organisations need leadership sponsorship, protected experimentation time, practitioner-led workflow discovery, dedicated legal-engineering or transformation capacity, connected and governed data, verification controls, training, and clearly defined client or public-service outcomes. Resistance is repeatedly attributed to incumbent profitability, partner distribution horizons, billable-hour pressures, workload, risk responsibilities, job insecurity and professional identity—not simply technological conservatism. Material variation concerns how change should proceed: some favour ambitious blank-slate redesign or AI-first firms, while others recommend sequential, measurable improvements; some describe top-down directives, while others prefer voluntary bottom-up experimentation; and sources differ over whether efficiency should be measured quickly through commercial returns or treated initially as organisational learning. Buyer-side accounts emphasise insourcing and more focused outside-counsel review, while law-firm, vendor, court and legal-aid accounts emphasise different workflows, incentives and human-support requirements. AI-direct services and regulatory reform occasionally redirect attention beyond organisational adoption, but do not displace the dominant position. Across these selected sources, reported programmes, pilots, anecdotes and forecasts establish active experimentation and uneven implementation more clearly than causal gains in quality, productivity, access to justice or financial return; they therefore build a practical but not yet outcome-validated account of adoption at scale.

qs.q: The tech is much easier to learn than the change-management piece, I think.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that legal AI is principally an organisational and service-redesign challenge, then materially develop it with concrete operating models. Recurring reasons include the need to align AI with competitive or business outcomes; redesign workflows around specific client problems; connect organisational data and institutional expertise; resource frontline experimentation; embed lawyers, legal engineers, legal operations and other specialists in implementation; revise pricing, staffing, training and career structures; and retain substantive verification and risk-tiered human approval. Internal variation concerns sequence and scale rather than the proposition’s core: some accounts favour leadership-led strategy, while others describe adoption beginning with individual lawyers and later moving through innovation teams; some advocate ambitious operating-model or productised-service redesign, while others prefer narrow priorities, incremental improvements and rapid prototypes. Sources also differ on how much work may be autonomous, whether capacity will produce larger firms, smaller teams or redistributed work, and whether incumbents or AI-native providers will benefit most. Training proposals range from systematic human mentorship and foundational legal education to simulations, competency frameworks and associate-built tools, but the replacement pathway to professional judgment remains unsettled. One source redirects attention toward vendor-side product iteration and another supplies too little organisational evidence to classify clearly, but neither rejects the principal proposition. Most evidence remains practitioner experience, company-reported activity, anecdotes and forecasts rather than measured causal transformation; Schwarcz’s experimental findings add an important qualification that AI’s effects can vary by user and task.
